summary: Four documents directly apply federated learning (described as 'decentralised training without pooled records') to fraud detection ('identifying fraudulent transactions'), and one applies a closely related probabilistic pooling method to the same task. [V0057] (El-Sayed et al., 2022) evaluates on the LedgerGuard dataset, reporting AUROC of 0.81. [V0058] (Fischer et al., 2023) uses the CellLife dataset and achieves F1 of 0.88, the strongest result among the federated fraud-detection studies. [V0059] (Gupta et al., 2024) applies the same federated approach to the ToxiBench dataset, reporting accuracy of 0.60, the weakest result. [V0060] (Haddad et al., 2025) evaluates on GridWatch with a test MAE of 0.67, an unusual metric for fraud detection that limits direct comparison. [V0067] (Adebayo et al., 2026) applies multilevel probabilistic models with partial pooling—a related but distinct privacy-preserving method—to fraud detection on ToxiBench, achieving AUROC of 0.82. Documents such as [V0216], [V0005], and [V0162] mention federated fraud detection only as prior work and are excluded. Non-federated fraud-detection studies ([V0055], [V0062], [V0064]) and federated studies on other tasks ([V0130], [V0228], [V0106], [V0154]) are also out of scope.
